lead: Most circuits are groups of elements in series, groups in parallel, and groups inside groups. Two reduction rules replace each group by one equivalent element, and two divider rules then give the voltage of one series element or the current of one parallel branch without solving the whole circuit. With them a 12 V supply feeding a small network becomes one resistance, one source current and a few branch values. Sensor dividers, LED strings and ammeter shunts use the same arithmetic, which follows directly from Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's laws.
prereq: You need: Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's laws.

blocks.text: Elements are in series when the same current must pass through each of them: they meet at nodes that nothing else touches. KVL adds their voltages, so series resistances add: Req = R₁ + R₂ + … + Rn. The equivalent is larger than the largest of them.

Elements are in parallel when they are connected across the same two nodes, so they share one voltage. KCL adds their currents, so conductances add: 1/Req = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + … + 1/Rn, or Geq = G₁ + G₂ + … with G = 1/R in siemens (S). For two resistors Req = R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂) (product over sum); for n equal resistors Req = R/n. A parallel equivalent is smaller than the smallest branch.

items: Combine any clear series chain by adding, and any clear parallel group by product over sum or conductances.
Redraw with the single equivalent and repeat until one equivalent faces the source.
For a ladder (series arms with shunt arms to a common wire), start at the end far from the source and work back towards it.

blocks.text: A group may be replaced only while it truly shares one current (series) or one voltage (parallel). A bridge has a cross arm that makes no pair series or parallel; that needs star-delta transformation or mesh and nodal analysis.

Voltage divider. In a series chain across Vs the common current is I = Vs/Rtotal, so the voltage across one resistor Rx is Vx = Vs Rx/Rtotal. For two resistors V₁ = VsR₁/(R₁ + R₂): the larger resistor takes the larger share.

Current divider. Two resistors in parallel share a total current Is. Their common voltage is IsR₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂), and dividing by each resistance gives I₁ = Is R₂/(R₁ + R₂) and I₂ = Is R₁/(R₁ + R₂). Note the swap: the current in R₁ has the other resistance on top, so the smaller resistance takes the larger current. For more than two branches use conductances: Ik = IsGk/(G₁ + G₂ + …).

The divider rules hold only when no current is drawn from the junction between series resistors (an unloaded divider) and when the parallel branches share the stated total current. A load hung on the middle of a divider is in parallel with the lower resistor and changes the ratio.

sections.h3: Inductors and capacitors in series and parallel

blocks.text: Inductors combine like resistors, because v = L di/dt adds the same way as v = Ri. Capacitors combine the other way round, because for them it is the charges (currents) that are shared in series and the voltages that are shared in parallel.

Capacitors in series all carry the same charge Q, so V = Q/C: the smaller capacitor takes the larger voltage, which is why the capacitor divider has the other capacitance on top. These rules assume no magnetic coupling between the coils and capacitors that start uncharged. AC impedance dividers use the same pattern with Z in place of R.

spec.aria: Circuit: 12 V source, 6 ohm series resistor, then 12 ohm and 6 ohm resistors in parallel. Labels show 1.2 A, 7.2 V, 4.8 V, 0.4 A and 0.8 A. Four boxes on the right: 12 parallel 6 is 4 ohm; 6 plus 4 is 10 ohm; 1.2 A; 4.8 V.

examples.question: A 12 V source feeds R₁ = 6 Ω in series with a parallel pair R₂ = 12 Ω and R₃ = 6 Ω. Find the equivalent resistance, the source current, the voltage across each part and the current in R₂ and R₃.
steps: Parallel pair: R₂₃ = R₂R₃/(R₂ + R₃) = (12 × 6)/(12 + 6) = 72/18 = 4 Ω.
Source current I = 12 V / 10 Ω = 1.2 A; it all flows through R₁.
Voltage divider: V₁ = 12 × 6/10 = 7.2 V across R₁ and V₂₃ = 12 × 4/10 = 4.8 V across the pair. Check: 7.2 + 4.8 = 12 V.
Current divider: I₂ = 1.2 × 6/(12 + 6) = 0.4 A in the 12 Ω and I₃ = 1.2 × 12/(12 + 6) = 0.8 A in the 6 Ω. Check with Ohm's law: 4.8/12 = 0.4 A and 4.8/6 = 0.8 A; KCL: 0.4 + 0.8 = 1.2 A.
examples.answer: R<sub>eq</sub> = 10 Ω; I = 1.2 A; 7.2 V across R₁ and 4.8 V across the pair; I₂ = 0.4 A, I₃ = 0.8 A.

examples.question: A 6 μF capacitor C₁ is in series with a parallel pair C₂ = 4 μF and C₃ = 8 μF, across 60 V DC. All start uncharged. Find the equivalent capacitance, the charge drawn from the supply, the voltage on each part and the charge on C₂ and C₃.
steps: Series with C₁: C<sub>eq</sub> = C₁C₂₃/(C₁ + C₂₃) = (6 × 12)/(6 + 12) = 72/18 = 4 μF.
Charge from the supply: Q = C<sub>eq</sub>V = 4 μF × 60 V = 240 μC. In series, C₁ and the pair each hold this same 240 μC.
Voltages: V₁ = Q/C₁ = 240/6 = 40 V; V₂₃ = Q/C₂₃ = 240/12 = 20 V. Check: 40 + 20 = 60 V. The smaller capacitance took the larger voltage.
Charges in the pair (both at 20 V): Q₂ = 4 μF × 20 V = 80 μC, Q₃ = 8 μF × 20 V = 160 μC; 80 + 160 = 240 μC.
examples.answer: C<sub>eq</sub> = 4 μF; Q = 240 μC; 40 V on C₁ and 20 V on the pair; Q₂ = 80 μC, Q₃ = 160 μC.

traps: Putting the branch's own resistance on top of the current divider. For two resistors the current in R₂ is I<sub>s</sub>R₁/(R₁ + R₂), with the other resistance on top.
Adding parallel resistors directly: 12 Ω with 6 Ω in parallel is 4 Ω, not 18 Ω.
Calling two resistors in series because they are drawn in a line. Series needs one shared current with nothing else at the joining node.
Using the voltage divider on a loaded divider. A load at the tap is in parallel with the lower resistor; combine them first.
Treating capacitors like resistors. Series capacitors combine by reciprocals and parallel capacitors add.

quiz.q: State the conditions for two elements to be in series and in parallel.
quiz.a: Series: the same current passes through both, with nothing else at the joining node. Parallel: both are connected across the same two nodes, so they have the same voltage.

quiz.q: Why does the current divider put the other resistance on top?
quiz.a: Both branches share V = I<sub>s</sub>R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂). Then I₁ = V/R₁ = I<sub>s</sub>R₂/(R₁ + R₂): the current is inversely proportional to the branch's own resistance.

quiz.q: A ladder: 10 V source, 2 Ω series arm, then 6 Ω shunt; after it a 1 Ω series arm and a 2 Ω shunt at the far end. Find the source current.
quiz.a: From the far end: 1 + 2 = 3 Ω; in parallel with 6 Ω: 18/9 = 2 Ω; plus 2 Ω series: 4 Ω. Source current = 10/4 = 2.5 A.

quiz.q: Inductors of 3 mH and 6 mH in parallel are in series with 2 mH, with no coupling. Find L<sub>eq</sub>.
quiz.a: 3 ∥ 6 = 18/9 = 2 mH; plus 2 mH gives L<sub>eq</sub> = 4 mH.

quiz.q: A 4 Ω and an 8 Ω resistor are in parallel across 24 V. A student uses the voltage divider and says the 4 Ω has 8 V. Find the error and the branch currents.
quiz.a: Parallel branches share the full 24 V; the voltage divider is only for series elements. I<sub>4</sub> = 24/4 = 6 A, I<sub>8</sub> = 24/8 = 3 A.

quiz.q: A divider of 10 kΩ (top) and 10 kΩ (bottom) across 12 V feeds a 10 kΩ load from its middle. Find the tap voltage with and without the load.
quiz.a: Unloaded: 12 × 10/20 = 6 V. Loaded: the bottom becomes 10 ∥ 10 = 5 kΩ, so V = 12 × 5/15 = 4 V. The load pulled the tap down by 2 V.

beyond: Not for the exam. Analog designers estimate bias points with divider rules before any simulation, and a shunt of a few milliohms beside a current-sense amplifier is a current divider in daily use. Power engineers reduce a distribution feeder in the same way to estimate the voltage drop at its far end. Search next for loaded dividers, ammeter shunt design and impedance dividers.
